question: If I'm held in jail awaiting trial, how long can I be held before I must be indicted and tried, and what happens if that deadline passes?

groups: waive the right to be accused by indictment
first Mondays in January and July
failure to provide a speedy trial

gold_sections.why: The indictment clock: for a defendant jailed or on bail, the prosecution shall be dismissed and bail discharged if no indictment or information is presented by the later of the last day of the next term of court after commitment or the 180th day after commitment, unless the court orders otherwise for good cause shown by affidavit; a surety may move only to discharge the bail (so the dismissal is raised by motion, not automatic).

The remedy for a speedy-trial violation: if a motion to set aside the charge for failure to provide a speedy trial is sustained, the court shall discharge the defendant, and the discharge bars further prosecution for that offense and same-transaction offenses.
A 32.01 dismissal is not a permanent bar: the defendant may be rearrested for the same conduct only on a later indictment or information and a capias issued after it.
The statutory right to a speedy public trial, and the rule that a felony must be prosecuted on a grand jury indictment (subject to waiver under Article 1.141).
A defendant with a lawyer may waive indictment for any non-capital felony and be charged by information, which is why the 32.01 clock runs to 'indictment or information' for felonies too.

The first statutory limit on how long a person can be held: after a warrantless arrest, release on bond (not over $5,000) within 24 hours for a misdemeanor or (not over $10,000) within 48 hours for a felony if no magistrate has determined probable cause, extendable to 72 hours on the State's application.
Trial priorities: insofar as practicable, trials of defendants detained in jail get preference over other criminal trials (after child-victim and restored-competency cases).

The general ban on personal bonds for violent and certain other offenses (b-2) does not apply to release under Article 17.151 (or 17.033), the only text in the downloaded file that can be quoted about 17.151.

What a district court 'term' is for the 32.01 deadline: terms begin the first Mondays in January and July (in Harris County, February, May, August and November; Armstrong County's 47th District Court has one January term) and are continuous.
Terms of statutory county courts (county courts at law, which try many misdemeanors): at least two a year, set by the commissioners court.

Terms of the constitutional county court: fixed by commissioners court order, including the four terms the constitution requires (many counties' terms are also set by county-specific statutes in Government Code chapter 26, subchapter C, which the commissioners court may change under this section).

answer:
Texas sets a deadline to charge you but no general deadline to try you.

Charging: if you are jailed or bailed, an indictment or information is due by the later of the end of the court's next term or 180 days after [N1]. A felony needs a grand jury indictment [N4] unless you, with a lawyer, waive it (not in capital cases) [N5]. District court terms start in January and July (quarterly in Harris County) [N12][N13]; county court terms are set by commissioners court order or county-specific statute [N14][N15]. If the deadline passes, you or your lawyer can move to dismiss and discharge bail, which the court must grant unless the State shows good cause by affidavit [N2]; move before you are indicted. You can be rearrested on a new indictment or information and capias [N3]. After a warrantless felony arrest, you generally must be released on bond within 48 hours if no magistrate has found probable cause [N9].

Trial: under Article 17.151, if the State is not ready for trial within 90 days of your detention on a felony (30 for Class A misdemeanors, 15 for Class B, 5 for fine-only), you must be released on personal bond or lower bail, even on a violent charge [N10]; that is release, not dismissal. Where practicable, jailed defendants' trials get priority, after child-victim and restored-competency cases [N11]. If a court sustains a motion under your speedy-trial right [N6], you are discharged and cannot be retried for that offense or transaction [N7][N8].

out_of_corpus.what: When delay violates the constitutional speedy trial right that Article 28.061's discharge enforces: courts balance the length of delay, the reason for it, the defendant's assertion of the right and prejudice. Texas has no general statutory trial deadline because the Speedy Trial Act (former Article 32A.02) was held unconstitutional and later repealed; Texas's parallel guarantee is in its constitution
out_of_corpus.where: Sixth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution; Barker v. Wingo, 407 U.S. 514 (1972); Texas Constitution, Article I, Section 10; Meshell v. State, 739 S.W.2d 246 (Tex. Crim. App. 1987)

out_of_corpus.what: How an Article 32.01 dismissal is obtained: the defendant raises it by motion or pretrial habeas corpus (a surety may move only to discharge bail), and courts generally hold that an indictment or information returned before the claim is heard makes it moot, even if returned after the deadline, so the remedy must be pursued before indictment
out_of_corpus.where: Tatum v. State, 505 S.W.2d 548 (Tex. Crim. App. 1974), and Texas courts of appeals decisions applying it to Article 32.01 after the 1997 amendments; verify current Court of Criminal Appeals authority before relying on the mootness rule

out_of_corpus.what: How Article 17.151 works in practice: how the State shows it is 'ready for trial' (an announcement of readiness the defendant may rebut), that relief is sought by pretrial habeas corpus, and that a reduced bail must be an amount the defendant can make
out_of_corpus.where: Decisions of the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals and courts of appeals interpreting Article 17.151 (e.g., Ex parte Gill, 413 S.W.3d 425 (Tex. Crim. App. 2013))

out_of_corpus.what: Where bail is denied under Article I, Section 11a of the Texas Constitution (repeat or on-bail felony accusations and similar categories), the order denying bail is automatically set aside if the accused is not tried within 60 days of incarceration, unless the accused obtained a continuance. That 60-day clock governs Section 11a orders; it does not reach capital cases denied bail because 'the proof is evident' (Section 11), and the statutory no-bail holds under Code of Criminal Procedure Articles 17.152 and 17.153 ('pending trial') carry no statutory trial deadline; check Sections 11b-11d for their own terms

The actual dates of each county court and county court at law term, which fix the 32.01 'next term' deadline for misdemeanors: Government Code chapter 26, subchapter C fixes many counties' constitutional county court terms by statute (often quarterly, e.g. 26.103 Angelina County), but the commissioners court may change them under 26.002 and sets statutory county court terms under 25.0016, so the terms in force are in the commissioners court's orders
out_of_corpus.where: Each commissioners court's order entered on its records (Government Code 25.0016 and 26.002), available from the county clerk; county-specific sections of Government Code chapter 26, subchapter C

local_option: The commissioners court sets the terms of statutory county courts (Government Code 25.0016) and may fix or change the terms of the constitutional county court (26.002), which for many counties are first fixed by a county-specific statute in Government Code chapter 26, subchapter C (often quarterly and not continuous), so the 32.01 'next term' indictment deadline for misdemeanors varies by county; district court terms are fixed by statute (January and July; quarterly in Harris County; a single January term for the 47th District Court in Armstrong County) unless a disaster leads the regional presiding judge to designate terms (24.0125).
notes: Two different statutory remedies and one constitutional one. (1) Article 32.01: no indictment or information by the later of the end of the next term or day 180 means dismissal and discharge of bail unless the court finds good cause shown by affidavit; the dismissal is sought by motion or pretrial habeas (32.01(b) speaks of a surety's 'motion under Subsection (a)'), and case law (Tatum v. State, 505 S.W.2d 548 (Tex. Crim. App. 1974), and courts of appeals decisions) treats an indictment returned before the claim is heard as making it moot. Since 1997 this dismissal does not bar reprosecution (15.14 allows rearrest on a new indictment or information and capias; 28.061 no longer lists 32.01). With six-month continuous district court terms, the 'next term' date is usually later than day 180; with quarterly county court terms that run a few weeks, day 180 is usually the later date for misdemeanors. A represented defendant may waive indictment for a non-capital felony and be charged by information (1.141). (2) Article 17.151 (no row of its own in the downloaded file; text read from the anchor-only rows at CR.17.htm#1-#2; removed from gold_sections because its only citation, 'Code of Criminal Procedure § 1', resolves to Article 11.07 Sec. 1 in check-ask and the oracle arm and to 13 unrelated rows in retrieval scoring; once the parser gives anchor-only rows a parent-article citation, add it back as primary with a vital nugget for Sec. 1 and deadline slots of 90, 30, 15 and five days): 'A defendant who is detained in jail pending trial of an accusation against him must be released either on personal bond or by reducing the amount of bail required, if the state is not ready for trial of the criminal action for which he is being detained within' 90 days (felony), 30 days (misdemeanor punishable by more than 180 days in jail), 15 days (misdemeanor punishable by 180 days or less) or five days (fine-only misdemeanor) from the commencement of detention. Sec. 2 excludes a defendant serving a sentence for another offense, detained on another accusation whose period has not elapsed, incompetent to stand trial (during the incompetence), detained for violating a previous release condition related to victim or community safety, or civilly committed as a sexually violent predator. It only requires release, never dismissal. Gov't Code 71.0354(b)(3) makes prosecutors report the number of 17.151 releases, and Gov't Code 54.1356(a)(5) lets Cameron County criminal law hearing officers rule on writs of habeas corpus filed under 17.151 (pretrial habeas applications go to the court where the charge is pending, Articles 11.08 and 11.09). (3) Speedy trial (1.05; Tex. Const. art. I §10; Sixth Amendment): no fixed period; a sustained motion means discharge with a bar to reprosecution (28.061); the State may appeal an order dismissing a charge (44.01(a)(1)). Related clocks: a person arrested without a warrant must be released on bond (not over $5,000 for a misdemeanor within 24 hours, not over $10,000 for a felony within 48 hours) if no magistrate has determined probable cause, extendable to 72 hours on the State's application, with the clock starting at medical release for a person first taken to a hospital (17.033); a person discharged or bailed on habeas before indictment cannot be re-jailed for the same offense until indicted unless surrendered by bail (11.56); the Interstate Agreement on Detainers (51.14) is a true statutory trial deadline for people imprisoned in another party state: trial within 180 days after the prisoner's request for final disposition (Art. III(a)) or within 120 days of arrival in the receiving state (Art. IV(c)), continuances for good cause, and dismissal with prejudice if not met (Art. V(c)); statutory no-bail holds 'pending trial' for certain family-violence bond or protective-order violations (17.152) and child-victim bond-condition violations (17.153) carry no statutory trial deadline; competency restoration time is capped at the maximum term for the offense (46B.0095) and a restored defendant's trial gets preference (32A.01(c)); a detained juvenile's adjudication hearing must be set within 10 working days of the petition (Family Code 53.05). District court terms after a disaster may be designated by the regional presiding judge (Gov't Code 24.0125); Armstrong County's 47th District Court has a single term beginning the first Monday in January (24.012(a-1)). Many constitutional county courts' terms are fixed by county-specific statutes in Government Code chapter 26, subchapter C (e.g. 26.103 Angelina, 26.116 Blanco, 26.164 Dimmit, 26.261 Matagorda), which the commissioners court may change under 26.002.
